query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In an FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy protective coating, the presence of coherent interphase boundaries between the FCC and BCC regions promotes dislocation pile‐up under continuous loading, which in turn creates back‐stresses that suppress further plastic deformation and delay creep. In other words, these interfaces act as effective barriers to dislocation motion, enhancing creep resistance compared to a coating with less coherent or randomized phase interfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating exhibiting a dual-phase microstructure with distinct, coherent FCC and BCC grains and well‐defined interphase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply sustained mechanical loading (at a controlled constant stress and moderate temperature) that induces progressive plastic deformation.
generation.conditions: Continuous loading at moderate-to-high applied stress and a temperature regime where dislocation glide and limited diffusion dominate (i.e. conditions below the onset of rapid diffusion-driven creep or phase transformation).
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries that promote local dislocation pile-up and hinder intergranular dislocation transmission.
generation.mechanism: Under continuous loading, dislocations generated within the FCC (and possibly BCC) regions accumulate at the coherent FCC/BCC boundaries. This pile-up produces local back-stresses that restrain further dislocation motion, thereby delaying the onset of creep-related plastic flow. In a controlled comparison, a coating with reduced interfacial coherence (e.g., randomized phase distribution) would lack this effective barrier, leading to higher creep strain.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coating with coherent FCC/BCC interfaces should exhibit a lower incremental creep strain and longer creep lifetime under identical loading conditions compared to a baseline coating with less coherent phase boundaries. Microstructural analysis would reveal pronounced dislocation pile-ups at the interfaces in the high-coherence sample.
generation.baseline: A similar high-entropy alloy coating wherein the FCC/BCC interfaces are disrupted or randomized (for example, via a slight compositional or thermal treatment variation) so that interfacial coherence is minimized.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in stress and temperature regimes where dislocation glide and grain boundary interactions are primary deformation mechanisms, and before diffusion or stress-induced phase transformations become predominant (i.e. moderate temperatures and stresses below the thresholds that trigger diffusion-dominated creep).
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain to what degree other mechanisms—such as stress-induced phase transformations or grain boundary sliding—might contribute in overlapping conditions or interact with the dislocation pile-up mechanism. The influence of grain orientation variation on interface effectiveness is also not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy protective coatings with nominally identical compositions and processing history. In one set, employ post-processing (e.g., controlled heat treatment) to optimize and maintain coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries; in the other set, intentionally disrupt these boundaries (for example, through a modified thermal cycle leading to a more randomized phase distribution). Subject both sets to sustained mechanical loading under identical moderate stress and temperature conditions and monitor the evolution of creep strain over time.
measurements: Quantitative creep strain (e.g., using tensile or nanoindentation creep tests)
Dislocation structure and pile-up analysis using transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Interphase boundary characterization via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) or high-resolution SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings with optimized coherent FCC/BCC interfaces do not exhibit statistically lower creep strain rates or longer creep lifetimes, or if microstructural examination fails to observe pronounced dislocation pile-ups at the interfaces compared to the disrupted-interface baseline, then the hypothesis that coherent interphase boundaries are the dominant factor in creep resistance would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, MD simulations are conducted to systematically investigate the creep behavior of HESAs under varying stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction. The creep mechanism and the critical creep resistance factors are explored. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: The creep behavior of both HESAs and HEAs is strongly influenced by stress and temperature, and their combined effect governs the rate of atomic rearrangement during deformation. As these parameters increase, the creep rate accelerates rapidly due to enhanced diffusion and easier activation of deformation carriers. Temperature plays a particularly dominant role, as high thermal energy significantly facilitates atomic mobility, vacancy migration, and interface-mediated processes. Compared with HEAs, HESAs consistently exhibit lower creep strain under identical conditions, and the difference becomes more pronounced at higher stress–temperature combinations, highlighting the intrinsic microstructural advantages of γ/γ′-strengthened systems.
